claim: Lawson (1979) found that final-year architecture students used a solution-focused strategy (generate high-scoring candidates until one is accepted) while postgraduate science students used a problem-focused strategy (probe for the rule); a repeat with first-year students found no difference, suggesting the style grows with education and experience (Cross's review); Lloyd & Scott (1994) found experienced engineering designers used more generative, solution-conjecture reasoning.
agent_test: Compare an agent that must write candidate answers early and use failures to infer constraints against one that must list constraints first, on hidden-rule puzzles, equal token budget.
audit_note: Cross's review (listed as a02 and b03, one source) says Lawson's 1979 difference was between final-year architects and postgraduate scientists and was NOT found in first-year students; the 'later professional-style designers' link rests on Lloyd & Scott engineers, not architects.
claim_before_audit: Architecture students (and later professional-style designers) tend to generate and test candidate solutions to learn the problem, while science students tend to probe for the rule structure first. This is the solution-focused versus problem-focused split of Lawson.

claim: Lawson (1979) found no consistent strategy and no architect-scientist difference in school leavers and first-year students, whereas final-year architects and postgraduate scientists differed, which Lawson read as the style being learned through education; other researchers attribute it to specific experience or individual idiosyncrasy and no longitudinal evidence settles the cause.
agent_test: Not directly testable on an LLM; a style prompt is a scaffold, not a trait.
audit_note: Cross and Lawson (school leavers and first-year students showed no consistent strategy or difference) support it, but Restrepo & Christiaans explicitly say it is unknown whether the style comes from education, experience, situation or idiosyncrasy; the evidence is cross-sectional, not longitudinal.
claim_before_audit: The Lawson difference is not innate: first-year architecture students and school leavers showed no consistent strategy and no difference, so the style is learned with training or experience.

claim: Solution-first style is only weakly tied to quality. Problem-driven strategies scored better than solution-driven in Kruger and Cross and in Lemons et al. (qualitative, N=10), and Atman found more problem-scoping time did not help freshmen. Gap search: the Kruger and Cross abstract also says solution-driven designers scored HIGHER on creativity, so the trade is quality against creativity; effect sizes remain unknown (N=9).
agent_test: Run problem-first versus solution-first prompts on a design-brief set scored by blind raters at equal tokens.

claim: More experienced designers show more generative, conjecture-led reasoning and strong guiding principles (Lloyd and Scott 1994/95); novices spend more effort on information gathering and decomposition. Evidence is review-level with small samples.
agent_test: Check whether an agent with a stored guiding-principle list (a memory item) beats one starting from scratch at equal tokens.

claim: Experts do not scope broader in every setting: in the Midwest Floods task experts wrote about five times more statements (57 vs 11.5) but the design-detail versus context mix was almost equal (46/54 vs 48/52), and only 2 of 4 experts were breadth-first.
agent_test: Count scoping statements by an agent on a fixed scenario with and without a scoping step; compare mix, not only volume.

claim: Expert-novice difference in analogy: experts make more analogies per hour (32.2 vs 22.9) but mostly schema-driven (53.1 vs 16.5 per hour), while novices lean on case-driven ones (29.4 vs 11.3). N=16.
agent_test: Test retrieval of abstract schemas versus concrete past cases in a memory module at equal tokens.

claim: Process differences between experts and novices are small or null in some recent protocol studies: Chen et al. (2022, 4 vs 5) found no phase-sequence or total-time difference, only longer continuous design activity for experts (976 s vs 446 s).
agent_test: None needed; a reminder not to hard-code phase order.

claim: Fixation on an early concept is a measurable cost for human designers: example solutions raised copied features (Jansson and Smith 1991), and in a nine-group game the three best groups scrapped their first design and restarted.
agent_test: Compare an agent forced to produce a second independent design after a first versus one that refines the first, equal tokens.
audit: downgraded 2026-11-20 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: Seeing AI-generated images raised fixation on an example in human sketchers (GenAI +.32, Bayes Factor 124; image search +.27) and lowered fluency and originality; fixation carried into the next sketch (rho 0.56).
agent_test: Run an agent on a fixation task with and without being shown its own prior output.

claim: LLMs themselves show fixation: GPT-4o chair designs had fewer unique terms than Red Dot human entries (67.4% vs 78.2%), fewer structure keywords (142.71 vs 208.57 per 100), and image outputs were more clustered (16.05 vs 16.25 distance).
agent_test: Sample N designs per prompt with a diversity operator versus plain resampling; measure unique-term share at equal tokens.

claim: In a 48-hour hackathon a GPT-4 team ranked second of six (14.8 m vs winner 37.66 m, mean 12.0 m). It listed five concepts at once but dropped its pneumatic concept after one setback and fixated on the last item in prompt lists.
agent_test: Give an agent a retry-k-times-before-pivot rule versus free pivot on multi-step engineering tasks.

claim: An LLM prompted to act as a solution-driven or problem-driven designer follows the style (P-S index right in 20/20 and 18/20 runs; solution-driven SS transitions 29.4% vs 9.9%, t=-8.949), and style prompts raised novelty and integrity over baseline. It lacks human-like problem-solution back-and-forth.
agent_test: Replicate with another model; test whether forced alternation of problem and solution steps improves integrity.

claim: LLM help in problem reframing did not raise frame quality (N=280 analysed of 456, 15 expert raters) and widened the gap between knowledgeable and less knowledgeable users.
agent_test: Compare structured reframing prompts against free generation for an agent, equal tokens, rated blind.

claim: Novices tend to accept LLM output passively; role-play prompts (LLM as novice mentee in Feed-O-Meter, or as questioner) raised expert-rated feedback specificity (4.64 vs 4.34) and justification (4.73 vs 4.42).
agent_test: Test an agent that must question its own draft as a persona versus one that revises directly.

claim: An LLM rater of design ideas is more generous than humans with only moderate agreement (Pearson .556 with experts), and humans disagree among themselves, so LLM judges are weak ground truth for design quality.
agent_test: Measure agreement of an agent self-scorer with expert ratings before using it as a stop rule.

claim: Experienced UX designers beat GPT-4o on soundness of reasoning about latent user needs (about .42-.45 vs .298), so outcome checks can approve LLM output whose reasoning is weak.
agent_test: Score reasoning steps, not only final answers, for an agent on need elicitation at equal tokens.

claim: Multi-agent scaffolds copying the human meta-cognitive ideation loop (13 agents) yielded 11-24 final ideas from 50-80 raw per session, but no head-to-head quality numbers are reported.
agent_test: Match a 13-agent loop against a single call at equal total tokens on idea novelty.

claim: Solution conjectures change how designers see the problem; a computational model of expert teams needs fewer steps than novice teams (290.7 vs 379.6; 316.2 vs 494.7) with more new structures per step. Model results, not human data.
agent_test: Test whether agents with a conjecture-to-problem-update step reach a solved state in fewer steps.

claim: Solution-focus is argued to suit ill-defined problems that cannot become well-defined (Cross); no direct test shows solution-first is better or worse by problem type.
agent_test: Cross problem well-definedness with solution-first versus problem-first prompts.

claim: In rule-discovery loops (Wason 2-4-6 style), LLMs mostly test to confirm their current guess and less confirmation bias goes with higher rule discovery; counterexample prompts raised discovery from 42% to 56% on average (11 LLMs, Jhaveri et al.); on FalsifyBench the strongest reasoning models reached 68-75% (GPT-OSS-120B, GPT-5.2-Chat) versus 33-41% for instruction-tuned models, but small reasoning models (GPT-5-Nano 12%, Qwen3.5-9B 21%) did worse. This is the nearest LLM test of the Lawson hidden-rule setting; it does not test solution-first versus constraints-first order.
schema_part: O (test that tries to break the candidate); G (falsify before accept)
agent_test: Hidden-rule game: arm A writes a candidate first then must propose a test that would falsify it; arm B lists constraints first; equal tokens; measure success within 45 turns.
audit_note: Counterexample result (42% to 56%, 11 LLMs) and the 68-75% vs 33-41% figures are correct, but 68-75% are only the two best reasoning models; small reasoning models (GPT-5-Nano 12%, Qwen3.5-9B 21%) scored below instruction-tuned ones.
claim_before_audit: In rule-discovery loops (Wason 2-4-6 style), LLMs mostly test to confirm their current guess; less confirmation bias goes with higher rule discovery, and reasoning-mode models do better. Counterexample prompts raised discovery from 42% to 56% on average (11 LLMs), and reasoning models reached 68-75% on FalsifyBench versus 33-41% for instruction-tuned ones. This is the nearest LLM test of the Lawson hidden-rule setting; it does not test solution-first versus constraints-first order.

claim: Abstract strategy memory transfers across tasks more safely than raw case trajectories (forward transfer ALFWorld +6.5 vs -9.5, BabyAI +9.0 vs -7.5), but raw cases win within the same task (80.5 vs 65.5 success on task A). Single backbone, two environments.
agent_test: Same agent with schema memory vs case memory vs hybrid on near and far tasks, measuring forward transfer.

claim: Coding and ML agents pivot at the wrong rate and cannot reopen abandoned approaches: humans pivot on 25% of steps, Codex 9%, MLEvolve 58% with no net gain (-0.008 vs +0.089 for humans); agents almost never return to earlier lines (top humans 9% of versions, 78% of returns ended higher). A restart that carries the old diff beat a cold restart (71.8% vs 66.8% resolution). Supports a pivot rule that keeps a parked-idea note.
schema_part: S-state pivot with return; memory of parked ideas
agent_test: Compare persist-k-then-restart with carry-over vs cold restart vs no pivot on a multi-try design or code task.

claim: LLM judges track human creativity ratings only moderately (r = 0.50 over 1,103 ideas; Kendall tau about 0.50 in prior work) and ignore contextual information that moves human ratings (b = 0.18, N = 1,195 humans). No study was found that calibrates a judge to expert design ratings and uses it as a stop rule.
schema_part: G (do not trust self or judge scores as stop rule)
agent_test: Calibrate a judge on expert-rated design briefs; test stop-rule precision on held-out items.

claim: No published experiment was found that measures design fixation or problem-solution co-evolution in 2025-26 frontier reasoning models. An LLM in a 36-person study (ChatGPT 3.5) never reshaped the problem space. The evidence for frontier models exists only for hypothesis testing (K20).
agent_test: Run a fixation test (example-then-design) on a reasoning model with and without a forced reframe step.

claim: Largest human data are still small or non-experimental: Studer et al. (252 competition problems) give r(102) = -0.18 between number of problem-exploration patterns and better placement; no group of 30 or more experts versus novices testing breadth-first was found; Lawson (1979) group sizes and significance remain unknown.
agent_test: Not testable on an agent; treat human numbers as soft priors.
